pages.c01-p01: Know what hardware, software, data and information are, and what 'to compute' means
pages.c01-p02: Know what input and output devices are and give examples of each
pages.c01-p03: Know the three categories of storage device and the difference between storage and memory
pages.c01-p04: Know the main components inside a computer and what each one does
pages.c01-p05: Understand what the CPU does and describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle
pages.c01-p06: Know how codebreaking at Bletchley Park led to the first electronic computers
pages.c01-p07: Understand why computers use binary and convert between binary and denary
pages.c01-p08: Add binary numbers, recognise overflow, and use binary to decode a message
pages.c01-p09: Know the units of storage from bit to petabyte and convert file sizes into bits

q.q: What is hardware?
o: The programs that tell a computer system what to do
The raw facts and figures that a computer processes
The instructions stored permanently inside the processor
The physical parts of a computer system that you can touch
q.why: Hardware is the physical parts you can touch; programs are software and raw facts are data.

q.q: What is software?
o: The physical parts that are plugged into the motherboard
The cables that connect the computer to other devices
The instructions or programs that control the hardware
The raw facts and figures entered by the user
q.why: Software is the set of instructions or programs that make the hardware do a useful job; you cannot touch it.

q.q: Which of these is an example of application software?
o: An operating system such as Windows
A spreadsheet such as Microsoft Excel
q.why: Application software lets you do your work; the OS, utilities and user interface are system software.

q.q: Which of these is system software?
q.why: Utilities such as antivirus are system software because they keep the computer running; the others are applications.

q.q: A pupil types the value 16 into a spreadsheet cell with no heading. What is 16 on its own?
o: Data, because it has no meaning or context
Software, because it was typed in
Information, because it is a number
Information, because it is stored on a computer
q.why: Raw facts with no context are data; 16 could mean an age, a score or anything else.

q.q: Which of these is information rather than data?
q.why: Only the sentence gives the value meaning and context; the others are open to interpretation.

q.q: What does it mean to turn data into information?
o: Convert the data into binary 1s and 0s
Process the data and give it meaning and context
Save the data permanently onto a storage device
Print the data out so a person can read it
q.why: Information is data that has been processed and given meaning and context.

q.q: The verb 'compute' means to...
o: switch a machine on and off
store files on a hard disk
q.why: To compute is to carry out calculations; it comes from the Latin computare, to count up.

q.q: Whose name gives us the word 'algorithm'?
q.why: The 9th-century Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi gives us the word algorithm.

q.q: Why is a laptop with no programs on it described as 'an expensive paperweight'?
o: Without storage the laptop cannot be switched on
Without a network the laptop cannot run
Without software the hardware cannot do anything useful
Without data the processor will overheat
q.why: Software tells the hardware what to do; without it the hardware is useless.

q.q: What does an input device do?
o: Carries out the instructions in a program
Keeps programs and files when the power is off
Lets the user put data into a computer system
Lets the user receive information from a computer
q.why: Input devices put data in; receiving information is output and keeping files is storage.

q.q: What does an output device do?
o: Fetches and decodes the instructions held in memory
Converts human actions such as key presses into coded electrical signals
Converts the computer's signals into a form humans can see, hear or touch
Keeps programs and files so they can be used again later
q.why: Output devices turn the computer's signals back into something humans can sense; converting key presses is input.

q.q: Which of these is an input device?
q.why: A sensor measures things like temperature and puts that data into the computer; the others are outputs.

q.q: Which of these is an output device?
q.why: A projector shows the screen on a whiteboard, so it gives information out; the others put data in.

q.q: What type of device is a scanner?
q.why: A scanner takes a picture of paper and puts it into the computer, so it is input; some old notes wrongly list it as output.

q.q: Which device is both an input and an output device?
q.why: You tap a touch screen (input) and it displays information (output).

q.q: An architect needs very large, precise line drawings of building plans. Which output device is best?
q.why: A plotter draws large, precise line drawings such as building plans.

q.q: A pupil wants to record their voice for a podcast. Which device do they need?
q.why: A microphone captures sound and puts it into the computer; speakers and headphones output sound.

q.q: A weather station must record the temperature every hour without a person being there. Which device should it use?
q.why: Sensors measure things such as temperature automatically.

q.q: To decide if a device is input, output or storage, what is the best question to ask?
o: Is the device inside or outside the case?
Which way is the data flowing?
Does the device have any moving parts?
q.why: Data flowing in is input, out to a person is output, and kept for later is storage.

q.q: What is a storage device?
o: Hardware that keeps programs and files permanently, even when the power is off
Hardware that holds only the programs and data the computer is using right now
Hardware that converts mains electricity into the low voltages components need
Hardware that turns the computer's signals into a form humans can understand
q.why: Storage keeps data when the power is off; holding what is in use now describes memory (RAM).

q.q: What are the three categories of storage device?
q.why: The three categories are magnetic, optical and solid state (M-O-S).

q.q: Which category of storage is a hard disk drive?
q.why: An HDD magnetises and demagnetises tiny areas on a spinning disk.

q.q: How does optical storage work?
o: A laser reads the disc; parts reflect the laser and parts do not
Tiny areas on a spinning disk are magnetised and demagnetised
Flash memory chips store data with no moving parts
Data is held only while the power is switched on
q.why: Optical storage (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) is read by a laser beam.

q.q: Which storage device has no moving parts?
q.why: Solid state storage uses flash memory chips and has no moving parts.

q.q: Which of these is an example of optical storage?
q.why: CD, DVD and Blu-ray are optical; SD cards and USB sticks are solid state; tape is magnetic.

q.q: Which of these is an example of solid state storage?
q.why: SD cards use flash memory chips, so they are solid state.

q.q: What does it mean to say RAM is volatile?
o: It has no moving parts inside it
It keeps its contents when the power is switched off
It loses its contents when the power is switched off
It can only be read and never written to
q.why: Volatile memory loses everything when the power goes off.

q.q: The school computer crashes before Ciara saves her Word document. Why is her work lost?
o: It was only in RAM, which is volatile
It was on an optical disc, which needs a laser
It was stored in the CPU, which is permanent
It was only on the hard disk, which is volatile
q.why: Unsaved work is held only in RAM, which loses its data when the power goes off; saved work is on storage.

q.q: Which statement correctly compares memory (RAM) and storage?
o: RAM holds all saved files long term; storage holds files currently open
RAM holds files currently open; storage holds all saved files long term
Storage is volatile, so it loses its data when the power is off
RAM and storage both keep data after the power is switched off
q.why: RAM is short term and volatile; storage is long term and non-volatile.

q.q: A teacher wants a small, tough device with no moving parts to carry lesson files between school and home. Which is best?
q.why: A USB stick is solid state, so it has no moving parts and is portable.

q.q: What are the five jobs every computer does?
o: Fetch, decode, execute, storage and output
Input, process, output, memory and printing
Input, process, output, storage and data communications
Input, output, saving, loading and networking
q.why: The notes list input, process, output, storage and data communications.

q.q: Running a spell check on an essay is an example of which job?
q.why: The computer is checking data using a program, which is processing.

q.q: Sending data over Wi-Fi or satellite to another place is which job of a computer?
q.why: Data communications is sending data over a long distance, e.g. cables, Wi-Fi or satellites.

q.q: Which component connects all the other parts so they can communicate?
q.why: The motherboard is the main circuit board that everything plugs into.

q.q: What does the power supply do?
o: Stores electricity so the computer keeps working in a power cut
Converts mains electricity into the low voltages the components need
Keeps the CPU cool by blowing air across it
Sends data over telephone lines and cables
q.why: The power supply converts mains electricity from the wall socket into low voltages.

q.q: What would most likely happen if a computer's fan and heat sink were removed?
o: The monitor would show no sound
q.why: The heat sink draws heat away and the fan blows it out; without them the CPU would overheat.

q.q: Which component processes images and video and sends the picture to the monitor?
q.why: The graphics card makes the picture for the monitor and is important for games.

q.q: Which component converts digital sound into signals for speakers or headphones?
q.why: The sound card handles sound, and converts back again for a microphone.

q.q: Which component is described as the 'brain' of the computer?
q.why: The CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions and does the calculations.

q.q: According to the key terms, what does memory keep?
o: Only the operating system, which is never deleted
Input data, software in use and results of processing, for the short term
Created files and installed software, for the longer term
Information sent to the printer and plotter
q.why: Memory keeps data for the short term and loses it when the power is off; longer-term storage is the job of storage devices.

q.q: What is a Raspberry Pi?
o: A storage device used to carry files
A tablet that runs only Scratch games
A credit-card-sized computer that can be plugged into a TV
A type of motherboard used only in laptops
q.why: The Raspberry Pi is a tiny computer that can browse, play HD video and run programs.

q.q: Where is the operating system kept on a Raspberry Pi?
q.why: The SD card is the Raspberry Pi's storage.

q.q: What does the CPU do?
o: Stores files permanently when the power is off
Converts mains electricity into low voltages
Displays images and text for the user
q.why: The CPU is the part that interprets and executes instructions.

q.q: What are the three stages of the CPU's cycle, in order?
q.why: It fetches the next instruction, decodes it, then executes it.

q.q: Where does the CPU fetch the next instruction from?
q.why: Instructions are held in memory.

q.q: During which stage does the CPU work out what processing the instruction needs?
q.why: Decoding finds out what the instruction is asking the CPU to do.

q.q: What happens after the CPU executes an instruction?
o: It saves the instruction to the hard disk
It decodes the same instruction again
q.why: The cycle repeats over and over while the computer is on.

q.q: A function machine takes input 4, multiplies by 3, then adds 7. What is the output?
q.why: 4 × 3 = 12, then 12 + 7 = 19; adding first gives 33, which is the wrong order.

q.q: Why would a CPU get 33 instead of 19 for 'input 4, × 3, then + 7'?
o: It carried out the instructions in the wrong order
It ran the fetch stage twice
It used binary instead of denary
Its clock speed was too slow
q.why: (4 + 7) × 3 = 33; instructions must be carried out in the correct order.

q.q: What does GHz measure?
q.why: Gigahertz is the CPU's clock speed.

q.q: How many cycles per second is 1 GHz?
q.why: 1 GHz is one thousand million cycles per second.

q.q: Laptop A has a 2.4 GHz processor and laptop B has a 3.2 GHz processor. Which statement is correct?
q.why: The higher the gigahertz, the faster the processor; GHz says nothing about storage or RAM.

q.q: Why is writing a banana sandwich algorithm harder than it sounds?
o: A computer can guess missing steps but often guesses wrongly
A computer cannot follow more than ten instructions
A computer needs every step written in binary
A computer only does exactly what it is told, in exactly that order
q.why: Every step must be given in order because the computer cannot fill in gaps.

q.q: Where did Britain's wartime codebreakers work?
q.why: The codebreakers worked at Bletchley Park in Buckinghamshire; Hut 8 was a team there.

q.q: Which cipher machine did the German army, navy and air force use?
q.why: Enigma was used by the armed forces; Lorenz was used by the German High Command.

q.q: Which machine did the German High Command use for its most secret messages?
q.why: The Lorenz teleprinter cipher machine was used for the most secret messages.

q.q: What machine did Alan Turing design to find the daily Enigma settings?
q.why: Turing designed the electro-mechanical Bombe; Colossus was built by Tommy Flowers.

q.q: Who designed and built Colossus?
q.why: Older notes wrongly say Turing; Colossus was designed by Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers.

q.q: Which cipher was Colossus built to attack?
q.why: Colossus was built to attack the Lorenz cipher.

q.q: How many characters per second could Colossus read from paper tape?
q.why: Colossus read intercepted messages at 5,000 characters per second.

q.q: Why was Colossus needed at Bletchley Park?
o: Humans were too slow to do the huge number of calculations
The Bombe could not read paper tape at all
Churchill wanted a computer that could run any program
The Enigma machine had stopped working
q.why: Codebreaking needs vast numbers of calculations very quickly; work that took weeks by hand took hours.

q.q: Why is Colossus described as a 'function machine'?
o: It used gigahertz to measure its speed
It was built to do just one kind of task
It was the first computer with a keyboard
It could store and run different programs
q.why: Colossus was special purpose: analysing Lorenz messages.

q.q: Why is the Manchester Baby important?
o: It was the first computer to store and run a program
It was the first programmable electronic computer
It read paper tape at 5,000 characters per second
It was the first computer to break Enigma
q.why: The Baby (1948) was the first stored-program computer; Colossus is often called the first programmable electronic digital computer.

q.q: What did a computer need to become general purpose?
o: More switches and plugs to set it up
Writeable memory to store, load and run different programs
A laser to read its programs from a disc
A faster paper tape reader for longer messages
q.why: Storing programs in memory turned a special-purpose function machine into a general-purpose computer.

q.q: Why did breaking naval Enigma help Britain?
o: It let Britain build the Manchester Baby
It gave Germany's High Command false messages
It stopped the Lorenz machine from working
q.why: Supply ships crossing the Atlantic could be steered away from U-boats.

q.q: Why do computers use binary?
o: Binary uses ten digits so it can store more
Alan Turing invented binary for Colossus
Binary is easier for humans to read than denary
Their circuits can only tell the difference between high and low voltage
q.why: High voltage is 1 and low voltage is 0, so two values are used.

q.q: What is denary also called?
q.why: Denary (decimal) uses ten digits, 0 to 9.

q.q: In binary, what does a 1 represent?
q.why: 1 is high voltage or ON; 0 is low voltage or OFF.

q.q: How many different patterns can 3 bits make?
q.why: 2³ = 8 patterns: 000 to 111; 7 is the largest number, not the number of patterns.

q.q: What is the largest number that 4 bits can hold?
q.why: 4 bits give 16 patterns, 0 to 15; the largest is 2⁴ − 1.

q.q: How many different patterns can 8 bits make?
q.why: 2⁸ = 256 patterns; 255 is the largest number.

q.q: What are the place values of an 8-bit binary number, from left to right?
q.why: Place values double going left, from 1 on the right to 128.

q.q: What is 00010101 in denary?
What is 10000001 in denary?
q.why: The 128 and 1 columns are on: 128 + 1 = 129.

q.q: What is 40 as an 8-bit binary number?
q.why: 32 + 8 = 40, so the 32 and 8 columns are 1.

q.q: What is 100 as an 8-bit binary number?
What is 1 + 1 in binary?
q.why: Write 0 and carry 1, giving 10 (which is 2 in denary).

q.q: In binary addition, what do you write down and carry for 1 + 1 + 1?
q.why: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, which is binary 11: write 1, carry 1.
7 + 1 = 8, which is 00001000; every 1 carries to the left.

q.q: What is it called when the result of a binary addition needs more bits than are available?
q.why: An overflow error: the extra carry bit is lost.

q.q: Why does 229 + 53 cause an overflow in 8 bits?
q.why: 8 bits can hold at most 255, so 282 needs a ninth bit.

q.q: What happens to the stored answer when an overflow occurs?
o: The answer is rounded to the nearest byte
The answer is saved but shown in denary
The computer adds a ninth bit automatically
The extra carry bit is lost so the answer is wrong
q.why: The extra digit does not fit, so the stored answer is wrong.

q.q: In the 007 code (A = 1 ... Z = 26), what letter is 01101?
q.why: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, and the 13th letter is M.

q.q: In the 007 code, which 5-bit binary number stands for the letter E?
Why are 5 bits enough to code all the letters A to Z?
o: 5 bits give 25 patterns, plus a space
5 bits give 32 patterns, more than 26 letters
5 bits give 16 patterns, one per vowel and consonant pair
5 bits give 26 patterns, one per letter
q.why: 2⁵ = 32, which is enough for 26 letters.

q.q: What is a bit?
q.why: A bit is one binary digit, the smallest piece of data.

q.q: How many bits are in a byte?
q.why: A byte is 8 bits, about one character such as 'a'.

q.q: What is a nibble?
q.why: A nibble is half a byte: 4 bits.

q.q: How many bytes are in 1 kilobyte in this course?
q.why: Each unit is 1024 (2¹⁰) of the unit below; strictly 1000 bytes is used on hard drive boxes.

q.q: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
q.why: The hierarchy is bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.

q.q: Which unit is the largest?
q.why: A petabyte is 1024 terabytes.

q.q: How many bytes are in 3 KB?
How many bits are in 2 KB?
To convert a file size from KB into bits, you should...
q.why: Going down to a smaller unit means multiplying: KB to bytes × 1024, bytes to bits × 8.

q.q: A file is 2048 MB. How big is it in GB?
q.why: Going up a unit means dividing: 2048 ÷ 1024 = 2.

q.q: Who worked on the electric telegraph and developed a dot-and-dash code?
q.why: From 1836 Samuel Morse, with Alfred Vail, developed Morse code.

q.q: What does Morse code have in common with binary?
o: It was used to program the Manchester Baby
It uses eight symbols for every letter
It was invented at Bletchley Park
It uses just two symbols to send any message
q.why: Morse uses a dot and a dash, showing two symbols are enough.
